context.title: Love as a test case
context.text: Arguments about lovers allow the dialogue to compare persuasive success with understanding of its subject. Verbal skill alone cannot settle that difference.
context.takeaway: Ask what each speech knows about people.

context.title: Spoken and written words
context.text: A written statement cannot answer a new question by itself. The dialogue explores what responsive teaching offers beyond possession of a text.
context.takeaway: Receiving words is not yet understanding.

notice.text: Notice Socrates correcting his own performance.
Follow the setting beside the river.
notice.why: Pleasure and inspiration complicate the discussion of rational persuasion.

opening: Phaedrus has found a clever speech arguing that a young man should favour someone who does not love him. Lovers, it explains, are jealous, unreliable, and likely to regret their generosity. Socrates can improve on the performance, but begins to suspect that cleverness has made them speak badly about something they do not understand. A walk outside Athens becomes an argument about desire and persuasion: what happens when someone learns to move another person's soul without first caring what is true.
